blocks.text: Standardization, the previous topic, rescaled each feature column independently, using that column own mean and standard deviation. Normalization takes a genuinely different axis entirely, rescaling each individual row, treated as a single vector, so that its overall length becomes a fixed, standard value, regardless of how many features that row actually has.

This topic covers the genuine, important distinction between rescaling by column and rescaling by row, what unit length actually means for a row treated as a vector, the two common ways to measure that length, L1 and L2 norms, why this technique connects directly back to the TF-IDF vectors covered in the Text Features topic, and specifically when normalization genuinely makes sense versus when it genuinely does not.
1. Row Wise Versus Column Wise Rescaling

blocks.alt: Standardization rescales column wise while normalization rescales row wise

blocks.text: Standardization genuinely operates one column at a time, computing a mean and standard deviation across every row for that single feature, then rescaling that column using those two numbers. Normalization genuinely operates in the opposite direction, one row at a time, treating every feature value in that row together as a single vector, and rescaling the whole row so its overall length matches a fixed target.

This distinction is genuinely easy to blur together, both techniques rescale numbers, but they operate along fundamentally different axes of the same dataset, and mixing them up leads to a transformation that does not do what was actually intended.

blocks.text: 2. What Unit Length Genuinely Means

blocks.alt: A vector gets rescaled to a length of exactly 1

blocks.text: Treating a single row genuine feature values as a vector, a point in a multi dimensional space, that vector has both a direction and a length. Normalization rescales that vector so its genuine length becomes exactly one, while leaving its direction completely unchanged, only how far the vector stretches gets adjusted, not which way it points.

This matters specifically in contexts where the direction a row points in genuinely carries the real meaning, and the raw magnitude is more of an incidental detail, exactly the case with the text vectors covered later in this topic.
3. Two Genuine Ways to Measure Length: L1 and L2

blocks.alt: A vector can be measured by L1, the sum of absolute values, or L2, the Euclidean length

blocks.text: The L2 norm, the more commonly used of the two, measures a vector length the genuinely familiar, straight line, Euclidean way, the same distance formula covered implicitly back in the discussion of distance based algorithms in Standardization. The L1 norm instead measures length as the genuine sum of the absolute values of every element, a different, though related, notion of size.

Choosing between them genuinely depends on the specific downstream use, L2 normalization is the standard choice for cosine similarity, covered directly in the next section, while L1 normalization is occasionally preferred when a genuinely sparse, count based representation is involved.
4. A Worked Example
Normalizing a small set of rows with scikit-learn Normalizer shows the row wise rescaling directly, in contrast to the column wise StandardScaler from the previous topic.

code.content:
from sklearn.preprocessing import Normalizer
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "feature_a": [3, 6, 1],
    "feature_b": [4, 8, 0],
})

normalizer = Normalizer(norm="l2")
normalized = normalizer.fit_transform(df)

print(pd.DataFrame(normalized, columns=df.columns))

blocks.text: Notice that the first two rows, 3 and 4, and 6 and 8, point in exactly the same genuine direction, one is simply twice as long as the other, and normalization genuinely rescales both down to the identical unit length, revealing that shared direction clearly.

blocks.title: A practical habit
blocks.content: Always double check whether Normalizer, row wise, or StandardScaler, column wise, is genuinely the right tool before applying either. Reaching for the wrong axis produces a transformation that runs without error but does not do what was actually intended.

blocks.text: 5. Connecting Back to Text Features

blocks.alt: A bag of words vector becomes a normalized vector

blocks.text: This technique connects directly back to the TF-IDF vectors covered in the Text Features topic earlier in this course, comparing two documents by cosine similarity, a genuinely standard technique in text analysis, specifically measures the angle between their vectors, ignoring raw length entirely. Normalizing every TF-IDF vector to unit length beforehand is exactly what makes that angle based comparison work correctly and consistently.

Without normalization, a genuinely longer document, simply containing more words overall, would produce a vector with a larger raw magnitude, and a naive comparison would incorrectly treat that as more different from a shorter document, even if both discuss the exact same topic in the exact same proportions.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: Cosine similarity and unit length normalization are genuinely a matched pair. Whenever cosine similarity is used to compare vectors, normalizing those vectors first is almost always the correct, standard practice.

blocks.text: 6. When Normalization Genuinely Makes Sense, and When It Does Not

blocks.alt: When only direction matters, normalization is used; otherwise it is skipped

blocks.text: Normalization genuinely makes sense when a row represents a single vector where direction is the meaningful signal, text represented as word counts or TF-IDF weights being the clearest, most common case. It genuinely does not make sense for an ordinary tabular row like income and age together, since dividing both by the same row length would nonsensically mix two genuinely unrelated features together, destroying the real, independent meaning each one carries on its own.

This is a genuinely important, practical distinction, unlike standardization, which is broadly useful across most tabular machine learning problems, normalization is a genuinely more specialized technique, reserved specifically for cases where treating an entire row as one meaningful vector is actually appropriate.

blocks.text: 7. The Geometric Picture

blocks.alt: Any length vector projects onto the unit circle

blocks.text: A genuinely short vector and a genuinely long vector that happen to point in a similar direction both collapse down to the exact same unit length after normalization, revealing that shared direction clearly, exactly as the worked example above demonstrated with feature_a and feature_b. This geometric picture is worth holding onto, normalization is fundamentally about comparing shape and direction, not raw size.

This is precisely the opposite emphasis from standardization, which preserves each feature own relative differences in magnitude while just recentering and rescaling them, normalization instead deliberately discards magnitude information entirely, keeping only direction.
8. Normalization Versus What Comes Next

blocks.alt: Normalization is covered here, robust scaling comes next

blocks.text: Standardization and normalization together cover the two genuinely fundamental axes of rescaling, by column and by row. Both, though, share a real, common weakness, standardization is genuinely sensitive to outliers, and even normalization can behave oddly if one feature within a row is a wild outlier relative to the rest.

The next topic, Robust Scaling, addresses that shared weakness directly, offering a genuinely outlier resistant alternative to standardization for the many real datasets where extreme values cannot simply be assumed away.

items: Normalization genuinely rescales each row as a vector, unlike standardization which rescales each column.
A normalized vector has its genuine length set to exactly one, while its direction stays unchanged.
The L2 norm measures Euclidean length; the L1 norm measures the sum of absolute values.
Normalizing TF-IDF vectors before cosine similarity is a standard, genuinely common real use case from Text Features.
Normalization genuinely makes sense for vector direction contexts like text, not for ordinary tabular rows.
The next topic, Robust Scaling, addresses the real outlier sensitivity that standardization struggles with.
